summary: For ages 7–8, teach that light bounces off surfaces (reflection) by aiming a torch beam in a darkened space, first establishing clean redirection with a plane mirror, then deliberately extending to rough or dull/matt surfaces (paper, crumpled foil, a wall, black card) to show every surface reflects light to some degree — just scattered. Link reflection to seeing: we see non-luminous objects because light bounces off them into our eyes. The central correction is widening 'reflection' beyond mirrors, countering the instruction-induced 'only shiny things reflect' misconception. Mastery here is observational, not the formal law of reflection (angle in = angle out), which comes later.
misconceptions: Only shiny surfaces (mirrors) reflect light; dull or dark surfaces don't reflect at all.
An object either absorbs OR reflects light — it cannot do both.
Reflection (and the law of reflection) only happens with mirrors.
Black objects reflect no light whatsoever.
The Moon reflects light 'like a mirror' (forming an image) rather than diffusely.
Reflection is unrelated to everyday seeing — a special mirror effect rather than how we see all objects.

activities.title: Bounce the beam onto a target with a mirror
steps: In a darkened space, use a torch and an angled plane mirror to bounce the beam onto a chosen target or wall spot (aim at the target or wall, not into anyone's eyes).
Adjust the mirror's angle and watch the bright spot move, learning that light can be redirected.
As an optional extension, use the mirror (or two mirrors) to steer the beam around a corner to a hidden spot, like a simple periscope.
Describe in your own words what the mirror does to the beam (it bounces/redirects the light cleanly).
activities.insight: Light travels in a beam and bounces off a smooth mirror in a clean, predictable way — this is reflection.

activities.title: Swap the mirror for dull surfaces and compare the bounce
steps: Replace the mirror with crumpled foil, matt card, plain wall, then black card, aiming the torch at each in turn.
Watch whether the neat bright spot from the mirror breaks up into scattered light on the other surfaces: a soft, spread-out glow from matt ones, and many small glints from crumpled foil.
Predict before the black/dull wall swap whether any light will reach the target, then test and observe whether a faint reflected glow still lands.
Compare side by side: mirror vs foil vs matt paper vs black card, noting clean bounce versus scatter.
activities.insight: All surfaces reflect at least some light; smooth shiny surfaces reflect it most cleanly, while dull rough surfaces scatter it — so it isn't 'only shiny things reflect'.

activities.title: Sort surfaces by how well they reflect, and link to seeing
steps: Classify a set of everyday objects by how well each reflects light — a 'reflects best/most neatly' group (smooth shiny surfaces) and a 'reflects but scatters it' group (dull/rough surfaces) — in a 'can it reflect light?' sort, noticing that every object reflects at least some light, so the sort compares degree rather than presence of reflection.
For a dull object you can still see, trace where the light comes from: source → object → eye, and explain that you see it because light bounced off it into your eyes.
Give everyday reflection examples such as a mirror, a puddle, or a polished floor.
activities.insight: Reflection is how we see non-luminous objects: even a dull surface sends some light to our eyes, which is the only reason we can see it.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain: does a dull black surface reflect?
steps: Before switching on the torch in a dark room, predict: when I shine it on this dull black paper, will any light bounce off it and will you be able to see the paper? Say why first.
Shine the torch and observe whether you can see the paper.
Explain what the result shows about whether dull surfaces reflect light.
activities.insight: If you can see the surface of the dull black paper where the torch shines on it (not just a dark shape against a brighter background), light must have bounced off it into your eyes — so dull surfaces reflect some light too, not just shiny ones.

checkQuestion: In a dark room you shine a torch onto a piece of dull black sugar paper (not shiny at all). You can see the paper. Does ANY light bounce off it, or does light only bounce off shiny things like mirrors? Explain how you know.
checkAnswer: Yes — light does bounce off the dull paper; that is the only reason you can see it. ALL surfaces reflect at least some light. Shiny smooth surfaces reflect it best and in a neat beam; dull rough ones scatter it, but they still bounce light back.
